entry: [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] [[Thermonuclear weapon|thermonuclear]] aerial bomb, the most powerful nuclear weapon ever constructed and tested. [[Nikita Khrushchev]] ordered the project in July 1961, and [[Andrei Sakharov]] oversaw it. It was tested over [[Novaya Zemlya]] on October 30, 1961, yielding the equivalent of 50 megatons of TNT. With a natural uranium tamper it would theoretically have exceeded 100 megatons, but lead replaced the tamper to reduce fallout. Dropped by parachute from a Tu-95V aircraft, it detonated automatically 4,000 meters (13,000 ft) above the surface. The design was too large for operational use, though it influenced the early development of the Proton rocket.

Centralized Russian state, also called the Tsardom of Moscow, existing from 1547 to 1721. Ivan IV was crowned tsar and grand prince of all Russia on January 16, 1547, and the state is generally regarded as the first phase of Tsarist Russia. From 1550 to 1700 Russia expanded by an average of 35,000 square kilometers (14,000 sq mi) per year, including through the conquest of [[Siberia]]. The period included wars with the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]], Sweden and the [[Ottoman Empire]], and a dynastic transition from the Rurik to the Romanov dynasties. [[Peter the Great]] took power in 1689 and transformed the tsardom into an empire. After victory over Sweden in the [[Great Northern War]], he proclaimed the Russian Empire in 1721. [[Serfdom]] became entrenched during the period, binding peasants to land and lords.

Genus of large biting flies (*Glossina*, family Glossinidae) that feed only on [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]] blood. Twenty-three living species are known from the African continent and the Arabian Peninsula. Adults are 0.5–1.5 centimeters (1⁄4–5⁄8 in) long and fold their wings completely over the abdomen when resting, which distinguishes them from other large flies. They have a long proboscis and can take a blood meal equal in weight to themselves. As biological vectors of trypanosomes, they cause human and animal trypanosomiasis, with major economic and public-health consequences in [[Sub-Saharan Africa]]. Fossil specimens have been recovered from [[Paleogene]] rocks in the United States and Germany.

Public research university in Haidian, Beijing, China, affiliated with and funded by the Ministry of Education. Founded in 1911 as Tsinghua College with funds from the Boxer indemnity, it prepared Chinese students for study in the United States. During the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]], it merged with [[Peking University]] and Nankai University, returning to Beijing after World War II. The university has 22 schools and 59 departments and is a member of the C9 League. Its alumni include political leaders [[Xi Jinping]] and [[Hu Jintao]], and [[Yang Chen-Ning]], a Nobel Prize in Physics laureate. In 1952 the [[Chinese Communist Party]] streamlined it into a polytechnic institute.

Series of water waves caused by the displacement of a large volume of water, generally in an ocean or large lake. [[Earthquake|Earthquakes]] cause about 80% of tsunamis, but volcanic eruptions, underwater explosions, [[Landslide|landslides]], glacier calvings and meteorite impacts can also generate them. Unlike wind-driven waves or [[Tide|tides]], tsunamis have a far longer [[Wavelength|wavelength]] and arrive as a series of waves with periods from minutes to hours. The name comes from Japanese, meaning "harbor wave," and the older term "tidal wave" is disfavored by scientists. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed or left missing at least 230,000 people in 14 countries bordering the [[Indian Ocean]]. In his 5th century BC history of the Peloponnesian War, the Greek historian [[Thucydides]] suggested that tsunamis were related to submarine earthquakes.

Tongan maritime expansion and hegemony across Oceania, beginning about 950 and peaking between 1200 and 1500. It was centered on [[Tonga]] on the island of Tongatapu, with its capital at Muʻa, and its sacred kings, the Tuʻi Tonga, were regarded as descendants of the god Tangaloa. Subject chiefdoms brought annual tribute, called ʻinasi, to Muʻa after the harvest. Its power rested on a large navy of long-distance double-canoes, and voyaging extended as far as the [[Tuvalu|Tuvaluan archipelago]]. The Manuʻa islands of [[Samoa]] were considered sacred and remained under Tui Manuʻa rule. [[James Cook]] witnessed an ʻinasi ceremony in 1777 and recorded accounts of the Tuʻi Tonga kings. Historians rely heavily on oral traditions, supported by limited archaeology.

Reptile endemic to New Zealand, the only living member of the order Rhynchocephalia. Although it closely resembles [[Lizard|lizards]], it is the sole survivor of a lineage that was highly diverse during the [[Mesozoic]] era. Its closest living relatives are squamates, including lizards and snakes. Rhynchocephalians first appeared in the fossil record during the Middle Triassic and reached peak diversity during the [[Jurassic]]. Tuatara grow up to 80 centimeters (31 in) long and weigh up to 1.3 kilograms (2.9 lb), with a spiny crest along the back. Extinct on the mainland, the species survived on 32 offshore islands until its first North Island release, into the Karori Wildlife Sanctuary, now named Zealandia, in 2005. Tuatara have been legally protected since 1895. The name is Māori for "peaks on the back."

Large, low-pitched [[Brass instrument|brass instrument]] with a wide conical bore and valves. The tuba was invented in [[Prussia]] by Wilhelm Friedrich Wieprecht and Johann Gottfried Moritz and patented in 1835. Descended from the serpent and ophicleide, it usually has three or four valves, though some models have five or six. Adolphe Sax developed contrabass saxhorns in the 1850s, and contrabass tubas were built in the 1870s. John Philip Sousa adapted the circular helicon into the sousaphone in the late 1890s. The tuba forms the bass of the brass section in [[Orchestra|symphony orchestras]] and of brass, concert and military bands. Since the mid-20th century it has increasingly been used as a solo instrument, with concertos by [[Ralph Vaughan Williams]] and others. A player is called a tubist.

American conservative political commentator and host of *The Tucker Carlson Show* since 2023. He was a [[CNN]] commentator and co-host of *Crossfire* from 2000 to 2005, then hosted *Tucker* on MSNBC until 2008. He joined [[Fox News]] in 2009 and hosted *Tucker Carlson Tonight* until its cancellation in 2023. Critics cite his false and misleading statements and his promotion of conspiracy theories. In February 2024 he became the first Western journalist to interview [[Vladimir Putin]] since the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

County seat of Pima County and second-most populous city in [[Arizona]] (pop., 2020: 542,630). Spanish colonists founded it as a military fort, Presidio San Agustín del Tucsón, in 1775. The city was the capital of the Arizona Territory from 1867 to 1877 and remained the state's largest city until Phoenix surpassed it in 1920. It is home to the University of Arizona and known for its [[Optics|optical science]] and telescopes. In 2015 it became the first American city designated a City of Gastronomy by [[UNESCO]].

Day of the week between Monday and Wednesday. In ISO 8601 it is the second day of the week, after [[Monday]], but in calendars that begin with [[Sunday]] it is the third. The English name comes from Old English *Tiwesdæg*, meaning "Tīw's Day," after the Norse god Týr, who was equated with [[Mars]]. Most Romance languages name the day after Mars, from Latin *dies Martis*. In Japanese it is *kayōbi*, from the planet Mars. In the Eastern Orthodox Church, Tuesdays are dedicated to [[John the Baptist|Saint John the Baptist]].

Rock consolidated from volcanic ash ejected during an eruption. Rock containing more than 75% ash is classified as tuff, while rock with 25–75% ash is called tuffaceous. The ash lithifies into solid rock after deposition. Despite its softness, tuff has been used for construction since ancient times; the Romans used it often because it is common in Italy. The Rapa Nui people used it to make most of the [[Moai|moai]] statues on [[Easter Island]]. Tuff can be classified as either [[Igneous rock|igneous]] or [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary]] rock, and it is usually studied in igneous petrology. Tuff is often erroneously called tufa in guidebooks and television programs, but tufa is a form of travertine.

Sport in which two teams pull on opposite ends of a [[Rope|rope]], trying to drag the opposing team's marker across the center line. Teams typically have eight or more members. The sport was practiced in ancient [[Ancient Egypt|Egypt]], China, India and [[Ancient Greece|Greece]]. In China it was known as "hook pulling" and was used to train warriors in the State of Chu during the [[Spring and Autumn period]]. During the [[Tang dynasty]], [[Emperor Xuanzong of Tang]] promoted large-scale contests using ropes up to 167 meters (548 ft) long. It was an Olympic sport from 1900 to 1920 but is no longer on the Olympic program. The Tug of War International Federation governs the sport internationally and organizes World Championships. Ropes can break with a sudden release of energy, causing serious injuries, so safety protocols and engineered ropes reduce the hazards.

Turkoman chieftain who founded the [[Seljuk Empire]] and ruled as its sultan from 1037 to 1063. He united Turkoman tribes of the Central Asian steppes into a confederacy and led them in conquest of [[Khorasan]] and eastern Persia. After the Seljuk victory over the Ghaznavids at Dandanqan in 1040, he made [[Isfahan]] his capital. In 1055 he took [[Baghdad]] from the Buyids and relegated the [[Abbasid Caliphate|Abbasid caliphs]] to state figureheads. He also led campaigns against the [[Byzantine Empire]] and the [[Fatimid Caliphate]]. He was known for his adherence to the Hanafi school of Islamic jurisprudence and commissioned many mosques and madrasas. He left no heir, leaving a vast empire at the end of his reign.

Hindu Marathi poet-saint of the Varkari tradition and devotee of the god Vithoba, a form of [[Vishnu]]. He is best known for devotional poems called *abhangas*, which are popular in [[Maharashtra]] and many of which address social reform. Through his *kirtans*, group prayers with singing, and his abhangas he criticized social injustice, caste hierarchy and the misconduct of some religious leaders, and he faced opposition as a result. He is believed to have met [[Shivaji]], founder of the Maratha Empire. Scholars debate whether his teachings followed the monistic Vedanta of [[Adi Shankara]] or the dualistic philosophy of [[Madhvacharya]] and [[Ramanuja]].

Genus of spring-blooming perennial bulbous plants in the family [[Liliaceae]], with about 75 species. The name may derive from a Turkish word for turban. Tulips were originally found in a band from southern Europe to Central Asia, and Persian and Turkish peoples were the first to cultivate them, from the 10th century in Persia. Tulips probably spread into [[Anatolia]] with the Seljuks and became a symbol of the [[Ottoman Empire]] by the 15th century. Northern European diplomats to the Ottoman court brought them to attention in the 16th century, and they became the subject of the Dutch tulip mania of 1634–1637, a speculative investment bubble. Tulips were widely depicted in Dutch Golden Age paintings and became associated with the [[Netherlands]]. A tulip-breaking virus produced variegated flowers, and today's closest equivalents are the Rembrandts, named after [[Rembrandt]]'s paintings of admired breaks. Breeding has produced thousands of [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] and [[Cultivar|cultivars]].

City in northeastern [[Oklahoma]], the second-most populous city in the state (pop., 2026: about 419,000). It is the county seat of Tulsa County and the principal city of a metropolitan area of 1.06 million residents. Creek Native Americans settled the area between 1828 and 1836, and the city was incorporated in 1898. Oil discoveries made it the "Oil Capital of the World" for most of the 20th century. Leading sectors today include finance, aviation and telecommunications. Tulsa has one of the largest concentrations of [[Art Deco]] architecture in the United States.

Two-day massacre by white mobs of Black residents of the Greenwood district of [[Tulsa, Oklahoma|Tulsa]], on May 31 and June 1, 1921. The mobs burned and destroyed more than 35 square blocks of Greenwood, then one of the wealthiest Black communities in the United States. The Oklahoma Bureau of Vital Statistics recorded 36 deaths, while a 2001 commission reported estimates ranging from 39 to around 300. About 10,000 people were left homeless. A state commission, authorized in 1997, recommended reparations in its 2001 report, and a memorial park was dedicated in 2010. Oklahoma schools have been required to teach about the massacre since 2002.

Hindu saint and poet, devoted to the deities [[Rama]] and [[Hanuman]], best known for the *Ramcharitmanas*. Born Rambola Dubey, he is popularly known as Goswami Tulsidas. The *Ramcharitmanas* is an epic retelling of the Sanskrit [[Ramayana]] in the vernacular Awadhi language, and he also wrote the *Hanuman Chalisa*. He spent most of his life in Banaras (modern [[Varanasi]]) and [[Ayodhya]]. The Tulsi Ghat on the [[Ganges]] in Varanasi is named after him, and he founded the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple there. He started the Ramlila plays, folk theater adaptations of the Ramayana. His influence is seen in Hindi literature, Ramlila performances, [[Hindustani classical music]] and popular music.

Microblogging and social networking website founded by David Karp in 2007. Users post multimedia content to short-form [[Blog|blogs]]. Yahoo acquired Tumblr for $1.1 billion in cash in 2013. Verizon announced in 2019 that it would sell Tumblr to Automattic, the operator of WordPress.com. Similarweb estimated that Tumblr had lost 30% of its user traffic after a stricter content policy was introduced in December 2018.

National park in the [[Amazon rainforest]] in the [[Brazil|Brazilian]] states of Amapá and Pará, bordering [[French Guiana]] and Suriname. Declared a national park on August 23, 2002, with the collaboration of the WWF, it is part of the Amapá Biodiversity Corridor. It covers more than 38,800 square kilometers (14,980 sq mi), making it the world's largest tropical forest national park. Together with the adjacent Guiana Amazonian Park in French Guiana it reaches 59,000 square kilometers (22,780 sq mi). The uninhabited park is a habitat for [[Jaguar|jaguars]], [[Primate|primates]], aquatic turtles and [[Harpy eagle|harpy eagles]]. Its tropical monsoon climate has an average temperature of 25 °C (77 °F).

Saltwater fish of the tribe Thunnini, a subgrouping of the [[Mackerel|mackerel]] family. The tribe comprises 15 species in five genera. Sizes range from the bullet tuna, up to 50 cm (1.6 ft) long, to the Atlantic bluefin tuna, which reaches 4.6 m (15 ft) and 684 kg (1,508 lb). Tuna are among the fastest-swimming pelagic fish, and the yellowfin tuna can reach speeds of up to 75 km/h (47 mph). Tuna, opah and mackerel [[Shark|sharks]] are the only fish that can maintain a body temperature above that of the surrounding water. Commercially fished for food, tuna are overfished, and some species, such as the southern bluefin tuna, are endangered.

Biome in which tree growth is hindered by frigid temperatures and short growing seasons. Arctic, alpine and Antarctic tundras exist. Vegetation is composed of dwarf shrubs, sedges, grasses, [[Moss|mosses]] and [[Lichen|lichens]]. In the Arctic, the soil is frozen 25 to 90 centimeters (10 to 35 in) down, and winter temperatures average about −28 °C (−18 °F). Arctic tundra is also a polar desert, receiving only 150–250 mm (6–10 in) of precipitation per year. The soil is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus and holds large amounts of carbon as [[Methane|methane]] and [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] in [[Permafrost|permafrost]]. As warming thaws the soil, these gases are released into the atmosphere, creating a feedback cycle that contributes to [[Climate change|climate change]].

Chemical element with symbol W (from German *Wolfram*) and atomic number 74, a metal found in nature almost exclusively in compounds. It was identified as a distinct element in 1781 and first isolated as a metal in 1783. Its important ores include scheelite and wolframite. The free element has the highest melting point of all elements, 3,422 °C (6,192 °F), and the highest boiling point, 5,930 °C (10,706 °F). Its density of 19.254 g/cm³ is comparable with that of [[Uranium]] and [[Gold]]. About half of tungsten is used in [[Tungsten carbide|tungsten carbide]], a wear-resistant material for [[Metalworking|metalworking]], [[Mining|mining]] and construction. Tungsten also occurs in alloys, [[Incandescent light bulb|incandescent light bulb]] filaments, X-ray tubes and [[Steel|steel]].

Hard, dense chemical compound of equal parts [[Tungsten|tungsten]] and carbon, with formula WC. It is about three times as stiff as [[Steel|steel]], with a Young's modulus of about 530–700 GPa, and twice as dense. Its hardness approaches that of diamond and is comparable with [[Corundum|corundum]]. Sintered with [[Cobalt|cobalt]] as a binder, it forms cemented carbide used in cutting tools, mining equipment, molding blocks and armor-piercing bullets. Henri Moissan first synthesized the powder in 1893, and industrial production of the cemented form began between 1913 and 1918.
